prompt.context: Your client is the owner of Not-So-Poshtel, a chain of hostels located in major European cities. Growth for Not-So-Poshtel has been stagnant over the past several years. The new owner has seen a lot of press about significant growth in poshtels (or luxury hostels) and wants to know if she should consider transforming her hostels into the luxury variety. Luxury hostels are a cross between hostels and boutique hotels and can include perks such as more private bunks or rooms, trendy amenities, regular maid service, and tech-savvy features. All hostel locations perform at the same level financially. The owner's goal is to increase profitability.
prompt.question: Should the owner of Not-So-Poshtel transform her hostels into luxury poshtels?

clarifying_info.q: How many hostel locations does Not-So-Poshtel own?
clarifying_info.a: You can ignore the total number of locations and calculate profit per location.

clarifying_info.q: What is the discount rate for any investment analysis?
What is the cost to upgrade one hostel to a poshtel?
clarifying_info.a: The upgrade investment is $200K per hostel.

clarifying_info.q: Should I assume this is a perpetuity?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, assume a perpetuity and that profit equals free cash flow.

framework: Understand current financial performance of existing hostels (revenue and costs)
Estimate expected financial performance of poshtels (revenue and costs)
Calculate profit differential between poshtel and hostel per location
Perform NPV analysis using the profit differential as free cash flow, the upgrade investment, and the discount rate
Identify qualitative/non-financial factors that could affect the decision

questions.prompt: What type of revenue and cost information would you need for a hostel, and how do you think a poshtel would compare on each metric?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: revenue drivers (price per night, number of beds, occupancy rate) and cost drivers (rent, utilities, employees). They should hypothesize that poshtels charge a higher price, may have fewer but higher-quality beds, have higher occupancy, and incur higher utilities and staffing costs while rent stays similar.

questions.prompt: Given the following data, calculate the annual profit for a hostel and for a poshtel. Hostel: price/night $20, 50 beds, 60% occupancy; costs/month: rent $4K, utilities $1K, employees $5K. Poshtel: price/night $30 (50% more), 40 beds (20% less), 75% occupancy (25% more); costs/month: rent $4K (same), utilities $2K (100% more), employees $6K (20% more).
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate annual revenue as: price x beds x 30 days x 12 months x occupancy. Annual costs = (rent + utilities + employees) x 12. Profit = revenue - costs. Should then note poshtels are more profitable and that the cost to upgrade is needed before recommending the transformation.

math.setup: Revenue = Price per night * Number of Beds * 30 * 12 * Occupancy Rate; Costs = (Rent + Utilities + Employees) * 12; Profit = Revenue - Costs
math.answer: Hostel profit: $96K/year; Poshtel profit: $180K/year; incremental profit from upgrading: $84K/year

questions.prompt: Using a discount rate of 10% and an upgrade investment of $200K per hostel, perform an NPV analysis to determine if the transformation is worthwhile. Assume a perpetuity.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify free cash flow as the profit differential ($84K), apply the perpetuity formula (FCF / discount rate), and subtract the upfront investment. A positive NPV indicates the upgrade is financially justified.

math.setup: NPV (Perpetuity) = (FCF / Discount Rate) - Upgrade Investment; FCF = Annual Poshtel Profit - Annual Hostel Profit
math.answer: NPV = $640,000 per hostel — the transformation is financially attractive

brainstorming.prompt: What else should the owner of Not-So-Poshtel consider aside from financial factors?

categories.name: Internal — Staff
ideas: Would new staff members with different skill sets be needed?
Retraining existing staff vs. hiring new employees

categories.name: Internal — Customers
ideas: Do poshtels serve the same customer base as hostels?
Is there overlap between hostel and poshtel demographics, or would Not-So-Poshtel need to target a different demographic?

categories.name: Internal — Brand
ideas: Will customers be willing to pay a premium for a poshtel under the Not-So-Poshtel name?
Is rebranding required to reposition the offering?

categories.name: External — Industry
ideas: Is the poshtel trend a fad or a durable shift?
What is the competitive landscape among poshtels in European cities?

categories.name: External — Locations
ideas: Are poshtels more popular in certain cities?
Should the owner prioritize specific locations for transformation?

recommendation: Not-So-Poshtel should pursue the transformation from hostel to poshtel given an NPV of $640K per hostel
A pilot approach is recommended — transform one hostel first and validate assumptions before rolling out to all locations
risks: Different clientele — Not-So-Poshtel may struggle to attract the higher-end guest demographic
Branding — the Not-So-Poshtel name may not support a premium positioning and rebranding may be required
Industry uncertainty — poshtels may be a passing fad rather than a sustained trend
next_steps: Select which hostel to transform first based on market demand and location suitability
Prepare for transformation: secure financing, engage architects and contractors
Monitor the pilot's financial and operational performance and decide whether to extend the transformation to other locations
